data.title: Moody's Spares France a Downgrade, Cites Rising Yields and Social Unrest as Risks
data.description:
06:03 PM EDT, 10/23/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Moody's Ratings kept France's credit rating at Aa3, seven levels above junk and on par with the UK, avoiding a downgrade for a country grappling with surging bond yields, political gridlock and street protests, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing a Moody's statement.

The outlook remains negative. Moody's said slower growth and a higher deficit have pushed France's debt burden somewhat higher than previously expected, bond yields have risen more rapidly than anticipated, and widespread social protests could constrain efforts to reduce the deficit, the report said.

Moody's said its baseline assumption is that a deficit-reducing 2027 budget will eventually be adopted, possibly by decree, according to the report.

Bloomberg reported that France's National Assembly on Friday rejected the "receipts" portion of the 2027 social security budget bill, sending the original draft to the Senate.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who lacks a parliamentary majority, has proposed a finance bill aimed at cutting the deficit to 5% of economic output next year from 5.4% this year, according to the report.

data.title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Stocks fall, but tech shares steady after selloff; oil hits highest in nearly six months
data.description:
(Updates with closing US market levels)

* Wall Street stocks end lower

* Oil prices extend recent gains

* US Treasury yields up; France gets respite

By Caroline Valetkevitch and Marc Jones

NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Major stock indexes ended lower on Friday even as tech shares mostly steadied, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest level in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.

The Nasdaq eased. European shares also ended lower.

An index of semiconductors rose 0.4%. On Thursday, it posted its biggest daily percentage drop since June after a report from Meta Platforms ( META ) reignited worries about the AI trade. The S&P 500 technology index was also up 0.4%.

The S&P 500 energy sector rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia fanned fears over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where United Arab Emirates authorities also reported an oil spill.

Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%. Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher.

US Treasury yields rose after the benchmark 10-year yield posted on Thursday its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years.

"There are still all these headwinds in terms of sticky inflation," said JoAnne Bianco, partner and senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management in Chicago.

The 10-year yield remained under 5% as concerns about the durability of a rally in AI-related stocks lingered. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note was up 3.7 basis points at 4.99%.

AI SHARES MIXED

Investor focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ), three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street.

Meta shares ended down 1%, while Microsoft ( MSFT ) was up 0.7%. Shares of Alphabet and Amazon ( AMZN ) eased.

"After Meta's report, there's still anxiety over the AI trade to a certain extent," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth in Boston.

Investors also digested other corporate earnings news. American Express ( AXP ) shares fell 3.7% after it reported results and its CEO said the company had good momentum, but needed to become a more "agile and efficient" organization.

Telecom company shares, including Verizon, dropped after a report that SpaceX was in talks with cellular infrastructure companies about launching a US wireless carrier program.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34.

For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, notching its third straight weekly gain.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 3.96 points, or 0.35%, to 1,118.97. Asia's bourses steadied overnight, with South Korea's KOSPI ending its session higher after shedding as much as 4% earlier.

EURO FALLS

The euro fell and was down for the week, while euro zone bonds stabilized after recent volatility.

The euro has been hit by concerns about unrest in France and the country's budget problems. France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.

The euro was last down 0.21% at $1.1191.

European stocks recorded their steepest weekly loss since early September. The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.31% to close at 635.77 points. For the week, the benchmark is down about 1.4%.

French yields, which were down 5 basis points at 5.04%, have risen nearly 27 bps this week, the most of any major euro zone country and the most in a week since late May.

A selloff in French government bonds this week pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011.

(Reporting by Caroline Valetkevitch in New York and Marc Jones in London; Additional reporting by Chuck Mikolajczak in New York Stella Qiu in Sydney; Editing by Elaine Hardcastle and Rod Nickel)

data.title: Amgen drug combined with immunotherapy extends survival in lung cancer trial
data.description:
* Imdelltra patients lived median of 21.7 months vs 12.1 months for control group

* Nearly 80% of Imdelltra patients alive after one year

* About 21% of Imdelltra patients had serious side effects vs 10.8% of Imfinzi-alone patients

* Data was presented at the ESMO meeting in Madrid

By Deena Beasley

Oct 24 (Reuters) - Amgen's ( AMGN ) Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's ( AZN ) immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.

Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.

The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.

"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen ( AMGN ). He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."

Imdelltra's US list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.

The Amgen ( AMGN ) drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.

Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen ( AMGN ) had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.

Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.

Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the US National Institutes of Health.

Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.

Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.

Amgen ( AMGN ) said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.

Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.

Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

(Reporting By Deena Beasley in Los Angeles Editing by Bill Berkrot)

data.title: Couche-Tard proposes up to $8 billion offer for Cumberland Farms, The Times reports

data.title: China urges US to halt proposed expansion of outbound investment curbs
data.description:
BEIJING, Oct 24 (Reuters) - The Chinese commerce ministry urged the United States on Saturday to stop expanding restrictions on American investments in China, saying a proposed rule on sensitive technologies would disrupt trade ties.

The US Treasury Department issued proposals on Thursday to update its outbound-investment security programme, adding biotechnology to restricted sectors and expanding coverage of high-performance computing and hypersonic systems.

Beijing's commerce ministry said in a statement that the proposal "discriminatorily" widened China-related investment restrictions and intensified curbs.

It firmly opposed the US proposal and reserved the right to take unspecified countermeasures, it added.

Beijing also said the proposal would damage bilateral economic ties and ran counter to the consensus reached by the countries' presidents, who have met twice in the past six months.

The US Treasury has said the measures, which do not only cover China, are intended to stop US capital from supporting foreign adversaries' development of dual-use strategic technologies that could threaten US national security.

The US programme had already restricted certain US investments involving China in semiconductors, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.

(Reporting by Eduardo Baptista and Beijing newsroom; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

data.title: UAE's Ras Al Khaimah shuts all beaches as neighbours grapple with oil spill
data.description:
Oct 24 (Reuters) - Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after an offshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighbouring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah.

The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given.

The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.

All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said.

The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions.

Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said.

Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout.

Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' ( WYNN ) planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island.

The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027.

Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East.

Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday.

UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.

(Reporting by Eman Abouhassira and Maha El Dahan; Editing by Mark Potter)

data.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
data.description:
Oct 24 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.

In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican's buttocks.

Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president's appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:

TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY

At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a "bad job" explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low poverty rate, low unemployment, record highs in the stock market and cheaper prices for some food items.

But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.

Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.

The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has "a long way to go" to help working people.

"Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don't know how these young people make a living for their family."

RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE

Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory.

Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday.

Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.

Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.

Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire - also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine.

TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY

Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.

But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.

"I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special."

The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.

At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.

Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday.

Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.

FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS

Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.

But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.

"What the hell happened to France?" Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. 

Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump's recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia's invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.

"They'll end one way or another," Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.

TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC

Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.

This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.

At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted's physique, at one point saying his backside is "like a pile of muscle."

"Then I looked at his legs, and I said, 'Man, his feet are big.' Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, 'This guy's a monster,'" Trump said.

Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old."

Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.

Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.

"Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't."

That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

(Reporting by Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose and Jacob Bogage; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Edmund Klamann)

data.title: CULTURE CURRENT-Chase & Status on the upside of AI for music
data.description:
(For full picture story, see here: https://bit.ly/4zm8xlz)

By Sam Tabahriti

Oct 24 (Reuters) - Chase & Status have spent more than two decades chasing the next sound, amassing more than 2 billion streams on Spotify ( SPOT ) along the way. Their latest album, released earlier this month, "Generic Everything," is driven by a different concern: the fear that technology is making culture more uniform.

The British electronic music duo, Saul Milton (known as Chase) and Will Kennard (Status), say the record emerged from conversations about artificial intelligence, social media and the growing pressure for artists to follow established formulas rather than forge their own path. Still, they reject the idea that AI poses an existential threat to creativity.

Speaking to Reuters in London, the pair discuss originality, technological change and why they believe individuality will become more valuable in an age of algorithms.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Your new album is called "Generic Everything." It's a provocative title for a duo that's spent two decades building a distinctive sound. What does it mean?

Kennard: It sounds like an angry statement, but it wasn't really meant that way. When we were making the record, we found the rate of change in technology, the impact of social media and the fast-changing pace of AI really overwhelming and confusing. We spoke to other artists and friends who felt the same.

The danger of that was that our own work started to sound a bit lazy and a bit generic. We could see that in other people's work as well. It felt like creativity was being squeezed into a singular space.

"Generic Everything" was a phrase we wrote on a whiteboard in the studio. It was a reminder to think differently and not always take the easy route. It became a personal mission to avoid the pitfalls of just sounding like everything else.

Which track unlocked the album for you? Was there one song that made everything else make sense?

Milton: I think it was less a single track and more a movement away from the record we originally thought we were making. During the process, the sound palette we were working with changed quite dramatically. We moved away from one idea and into a different place.

Kennard: "Disgruntled" was probably the moment we realised what we wanted the record to be. It had this guitar-led, punky, live feel that was very different from where we'd been before.

That gave us the confidence to push further in that direction with tracks like "Tension".

If someone from outside Britain listened to "Generic Everything," what would they understand about Britain in 2026?

Milton: All of our albums are a kaleidoscope into what's happening in British culture at that time.

We love championing British music and we're very proud of being British. We believe Britain has the most exciting, cutting-edge, forward-thinking, future-sounding music of all time. We create genres, we create scenes, we create movements, and the world follows.

What drum and bass is about, and what hopefully our albums represent too, is unity. It's about all colours, creeds, races and religions coming together under one roof, having a good time and escaping the stresses of life.

A lot of people worry that AI will replace artists. You don't seem particularly worried about AI.

Milton: The fear now, if there is a fear, is the complacency that it enables.

Suddenly you can put in a prompt, type a few words and it spits something out. Whether it's good or not is another question, but the ease of it can squash creativity. Every change feels terrifying at the time. We went from vinyl and CDs to downloads, and from downloads to streaming. Every stage felt like the end of the world and every time people adapted.

When we started, everything was samplers, synths and mixing desks. Then suddenly everything became digital. A lot of music didn't sound great at first because the technology was changing.

Fast-forward 20 years and people have figured out how to make incredible-sounding records. I think we're still at the beginning of that process with AI.

What can't AI replicate?

Milton: Original ideas. Fundamentally, it's recycling ideas. It can make things polished, but it can't really think differently. Style is individuality.

Kennard: The aim of the game now is to break out of that box and do something different and original. This album is partly a rebellion against our own generic selves. We could have made another record that sounded like our previous records, but that wouldn't have been progression.

If AI becomes more powerful, what becomes the most valuable quality for an artist?

Milton: Conviction.

If you're a musician or producer and you're worried that AI is going to overtake your music, then work harder. Put more into the craft. Come at it from a different angle. If everyone's going left, go right.

What do you hope people take away from Generic Everything?

Milton: I hope people see it as an honest reflection of where Will and I are right now.

We deliberately tried not to repeat ourselves. We didn't want to make another record that simply sounded like previous Chase & Status albums. The whole point was to challenge ourselves and avoid taking the easy route.

I hope people listen to it from start to finish because that's becoming increasingly rare. Albums are still important to us. We spend a lot of time thinking about the order of the tracks and the journey they take you on.

More than anything, I hope people can hear that we're trying new things. It isn't about chasing trends or following what's popular. It's about pushing ourselves creatively and seeing where that takes us.

The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject's own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

(Editing by Yasmeen Serhan and Aurora Ellis)

data.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Saudi cities
data.description:
Oct 24 (Reuters) - The Saudi-led ​coalition fighting Yemen's ‌Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired ​by the Iran-aligned ​group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.

About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.

The interceptions came two days after the Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's defence ministry in Riyadh, facilities belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in the Red Sea city of Yanbu and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, where Saudi authorities said two people were killed.

Saudi authorities have not confirmed the reported attacks in Riyadh and Yanbu.

Aramco told staff to evacuate its headquarters in the Gulf city of Dhahran, six people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Thursday.

The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday it intercepted drones over Riyadh and Medina, not far from Yanbu. On Wednesday, the Houthis denied launching drones towards Medina after the coalition said it had intercepted drones over the holy city and Saudi Arabia's Eastern region.

The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa. The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

data.title: Earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally.

Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta and Lam Research ( LRCX ). Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners.

Three other hyperscalers -- Alphabet, Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) -- headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets.

"There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro. 

"Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain."

Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index up 11% in 2026.

HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT

Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict.

With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season.

"I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings."

Alphabet and Microsoft ( MSFT ) report on Wednesday. Amazon's ( AMZN ) results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays.

Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs.

"Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management.

FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW

Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel ( INTC ) and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade.

Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron ( CVX ) and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar. 

The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10% chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data. 

One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections.

However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then.

Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision. 

"Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

(Reporting by Lewis Krauskopf, editing by Colin Barr and David Gregorio)

data.title: Moonshot curbs hacking ability in new Kimi model as fears grow over AI-powered cyberattacks
data.description:
BEIJING, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.

Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model's weights - files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems - by November 4.

Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.

"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.

Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.

China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.

Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.

Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.

K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model's offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.

K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model.

(Reporting by Eduardo Baptista in Beijing; Editing by William Mallard)

data.title: Analysis-Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters' choices.

But this time, with Donald Trump's war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president's approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.

     As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.

Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans blame Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.

Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush's Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader's handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.

The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn't two decades ago.

"The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump's war and other policies," said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. "Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he's dealing with all this."

POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY

With Trump's approval ratings touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.

That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.

Chief among them was Trump's lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.

He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.

At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.

Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.

Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.

For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.

Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump's economic record and Democrats' ruinous alternative is clear."

'IT'S THE ECONOMY, STUPID'

Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.

And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - "it's the economy, stupid," as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters' choices.

Opinion polls for this year's midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump's signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.

Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump's international approach.

The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey "finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration's foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America's global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions."

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.

LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY

Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.

For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term.

But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump's capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.

Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.

"For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom," said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.

Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

(Reporting By Matt Spetalnick; Editing by Don Durfee and Daniel Wallis)

data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: Analysis-Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.

His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, eased sanctions on Russian fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to the polls.

Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters. Nearly 80% of Americans blame Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. 

US diesel prices rose nearly 10 cents a gallon in the latest week to an average of $6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Diesel in the last two months has become a central issue not only in the midterms but as a catalyst driving up already-elevated US inflation. The fuel is critical for farmers, construction companies, freight operators and more, and government data last week showed its rise was partly behind hefty increases in delivery costs, early-stage food production costs and even toy prices.

The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like Iowa and Kansas, where rising fuel and fertilizer costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump's core supporters.

Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign rallies across the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced $8 billion in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Monday.

The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel exports, has created diplomatic friction.

"The president tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here," said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania.

The White House attributed high diesel prices to "pre-existing issues," including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia's war in Ukraine, while defending Trump's efforts to ease costs.

"The President wants diesel prices to fall, which is why he has taken historic actions to save American farmers, truckers, and workers every hard-earned penny," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said.

SKEPTICISM AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS

One of Trump's most direct attempts to lower diesel costs has struggled to gain traction.

Trump signed an executive order this month allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel, typically intended for off-road use such as farm equipment, for highway driving while temporarily avoiding certain federal tax reporting and record-keeping requirements.

But the IRS has not eliminated the federal diesel tax, instead temporarily waiving related reporting requirements and penalties through year-end, leaving uncertainty for truck stops and fuel sellers.

David Fialkov, top lobbyist at NATSO, a trade group representing the largest US truck stop operators, said members appreciate Trump's effort to tackle diesel costs but that the guidance remains "murky" and carries too much risk. 

"I really don't see any of these dyed diesel announcements making a meaningful dent in diesel prices," Fialkov said.

Trump is also turning to federal payments to cushion some of the constituencies feeling the pain.

Government payments to farmers were already expected to top $47 billion this year, buoyed by commodity payments and $12 billion in tariff relief distributed by the US Department of Agriculture earlier this year. The $8 billion farm relief program would push the total to a record $55.4 billion, exceeding the previous high of $45 billion in 2020, when farmers received pandemic assistance.

The payments can help farmers manage higher costs and lost sales but do not directly address the market disruptions driving up fuel and fertilizer prices. They also raise questions about taxpayer spending to compensate producers for damage that farm groups say is linked partly to the administration's own trade and foreign policies. 

"This is the second round of emergency aid this year to address losses that were largely foreseeable," National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said. "Trade disruptions and rising fuel costs tied to conflict abroad have put family farmers in a difficult position, and one-time payments can't provide the stability they need to plan for the future."

The aid will arrive after the November 3 election, and likely not reach farmers until the end of the year, USDA official Richard Fordyce told Reuters on Friday. 

FRICTION OVER RUSSIAN FUEL

Some of Trump's efforts to increase diesel supplies carry geopolitical trade-offs.

His decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to restrict Moscow's energy revenues and limit its ability to finance its war in Ukraine has drawn bipartisan criticism -- and raised questions about whether the move will meaningfully lower US fuel prices.

Trump has defended the sanctions relief as necessary to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and to release American prisoner Stephen Hubbard.

As the administration's intervention efforts have failed to lower fuel costs, Trump has sought to shift blame toward Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskiy rather than the Iran war ahead of the elections.

Analysts say the Iran conflict has been the much bigger driver of the diesel price spike, disrupting global oil flows and refined-fuel supplies, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have helped tighten supplies but played a more limited role in the price.

"I sort of see it as a blame-shifting kind of scapegoating operation, more than a genuine attempt to moderate prices in the lead-up to the election," said Edward Fishman, director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

(Reporting by Jarrett Renshaw and Leah Douglas; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Deepa Babington)

TORONTO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Slate Grocery REIT ( SRRTF ) (the “REIT”), an owner and operator of U.S. grocery-anchored real estate, announced today that it has obtained an interim order (the “Interim Order”) of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice (Commercial List) (the “Court”) in connection with the proposed acquisition by EP/BRX Holdings LLC (the “Purchaser”), a joint venture between an affiliate of Brixmor Property Group Inc. and affiliates of Everview Partners, L.P., of all of the REIT’s issued and outstanding units pursuant to the terms and conditions of an arrangement agreement (the “Arrangement Agreement”) among the REIT, the Purchaser and 1001700324 Ontario Inc. dated September 27, 2026 (the “Arrangement”). The Arrangement was previously announced by the REIT on September 28, 2026.

Interim Order, Meeting and Circular

The Interim Order, granted on October 22, 2026, authorizes the calling and holding of a special meeting of unitholders of the REIT (the “Meeting”) to consider and vote on a special resolution approving the Arrangement. The Meeting is scheduled to be held in a virtual-only format on Wednesday, November 25, 2026 at 11:00 a.m. (Eastern time). Unitholders of record as of the close of business on October 20, 2026 will be entitled to receive notice of and vote at the Meeting.

The REIT expects to file its management information circular (the “Circular”) and related meeting materials on SEDAR+ on November 2, 2026 and to mail those materials to unitholders on or about November 2, 2026. The Circular will provide details of the Arrangement, the matters to be considered at the Meeting and the procedures for participating in and voting at the Meeting. Once filed, the Circular and related meeting materials will be available under the REIT’s profile on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca and on the REIT’s website at slategroceryreit.com. Unitholders are urged to read the Circular and related meeting materials carefully when they become available.

Other Matters

In connection with the Arrangement, the REIT has applied to the Ontario Securities Commission (the “OSC”) for discretionary exemptive relief from the requirement to obtain minority approval on a class-by-class basis under Multilateral Instrument 61-101 – Protection of Minority Security Holders in Special Transactions (“MI 61-101”) with a view to ensuring that the vote is structured in a manner that is fair to all unitholders. Under the REIT’s declaration of trust, holders of class A units, class I units and class U units generally vote together as a single class unless the business to be transacted affects holders of one class in a manner materially different from its effect on holders of another class. The REIT’s board of trustees has determined that the Arrangement does not have such a differential effect.

data.title: Democrat on US FCC urges broadcast industry to be more aggressive confronting the agency
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The sole Democratic member of the Federal Communications Commission on Friday urged the broadcast industry to take a more aggressive approach in confronting the Trump administration's actions toward major US networks and stations.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez called on the National Association of Broadcasters to address the administration's efforts to challenge broadcasters on a series of fronts, including a warning from FCC Chair Brendan Carr that US broadcast networks could violate their regulatory obligations by airing "entirely fake polls" before the November 3 election.

"This administration is running a coordinated, government-wide effort to reshape the media into its sanctioned messenger," Gomez warned, adding that Carr was seeking to pressure networks into not running polls the administration dislikes, which she said was not proper.

Carr, who has repeatedly faced pressure from President Donald Trump to crack down on ⁠US broadcasters and journalists, in April ordered an unprecedented early license review for all eight of Disney's ( DIS ) company-owned ABC TV stations.

A spokesperson for Carr did not immediately comment.

NAB President Curtis LeGeyt said in a statement that the group appreciated Gomez's "recognition of the value of local broadcasters and her commitment to the First Amendment principles that underpin a free press."

"We will continue working with her and all policymakers to protect broadcasters' rights," he said.

Gomez said the NAB had been "largely quiet through the first year of this censorship and control campaign" but that it had not stayed "completely silent."

An "industry confronting a coordinated effort to turn licensing authority into leverage over election-year coverage needs more than a couple of tempered statements," she added.

In April, the NAB said the Disney ( DIS ) early-renewal decision "creates ‌significant uncertainty for all broadcasters" and argued the "FCC must be careful to avoid actions that create further instability for the local stations viewers and listeners depend on."

The FCC also said earlier this ⁠year that ​late-night and daytime talk shows are no longer bona fide news programs ​that are exempt from equal-time rules for interviews with political candidates.

(Reporting by David ShepardsonEditing by Bill Berkrot)

data.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training after security overhaul, discloses flaw in widely used software
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defenses.

The disclosure comes amid concerns over the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software flaws, including in the guardrails meant to contain them.

OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models used a configuration error to gain limited internet access in September. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its defenses.

To test them, OpenAI had teams of AI agents try to break out of their restricted environments. It said the agents found previously unknown flaws, which it had fixed, and training resumed on October 1.

During that exercise, the ChatGPT maker found a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool.

The company said attackers could exploit the flaw by sending malicious data that lets them run their own code on affected systems, including those using popular web software such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy.

OpenAI said the root cause was fixed in Brotli's source code in February, before it was known to create a security vulnerability, but no new version was released at the time. Brotli has since released updated versions and published a public record of the flaw after OpenAI disclosed it.

Separately on Thursday, AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI's internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year.

OpenAI told the safety organizations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes.

OpenAI has been conducting a broad review of its AI models' activity since the Hugging Face incident in July, and has informed more than 100 organizations about incidents of unauthorized activity tied to its AI agents.

(Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru, Chris Thomas in Mexico City; Editing by Pooja Desai and Stephen Coates)

data.title: Russia, Ukraine agree on ceasefire in embattled town, to hold peace talks next month
data.description:
* Ceasefire starts October 27 to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations through humanitarian corridors

* US official says next three-way talks may come in couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland

* White House says Oleshky has 1,700 to 2,000 residents left, down from 24,000 prewar

By Steve Holland and Yuliia Dysa

Oct 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through US first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.

The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.

Amid a US push to organise new talks aimed at ending the 4-1/2-year-old war, Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland.

Zelenskiy said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow.

Previous rounds of talks headed by the United ​States ​stalled in February ⁠with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas ​region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.

The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia.

A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest US midterm elections.

On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America.

In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis.

"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.

The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on October 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.

Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already used drones twice to send food into the town.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27 and told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians.

MELANIA TRUMP'S DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS

Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.

"Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.

"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water."

Pope Leo had spoken in the past week both to Zelenskiy and to Russian President Vladimir Putin about conditions in Oleshky.

The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war.

US ENVOYS

Zelenskiy's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St Petersburg.

Zelenskiy said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and US envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army.

"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskiy told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialised.

Zelenskiy spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks.

Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required.

"If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since October 13.

Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Zelenskiy described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result."

Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago.

(Reporting by Steve Holland and Andrea Shalal in Washington, Yuliia Dysa in Kyiv and Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Edmund Klamann and Stephen Coates)

data.title: Exclusive-Boeing supplier dispute has halted 777 freighter production for two months, sources say
data.description:
SEATTLE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Boeing's ( BA ) dispute with a small Florida-based supplier has halted production of its 777 freighter for nearly two months and disrupted output of the 767, including freighters and KC-46 aerial refueling tankers, according to Boeing ( BA ) workers and court filings.

Boeing ( BA ) filed a complaint in August alleging supplier Vaero had stopped delivering a critical wing component known as the trailing-edge rib kit, stalling work at the Everett, Washington, wing-production facility that supports the 777 freighter and 767 programs, according to a copy of the complaint reviewed by Reuters. The disruption was costing Boeing ( BA ) as much as $6.5 million a day, the complaint said.

Boeing ( BA ) said in the complaint that the trailing-edge rib kit was an "indispensable" part and Vaero was the sole supplier.

Although the companies reached a settlement in late September, production of the 777 freighter has yet to resume, according to three Boeing ( BA ) workers familiar with the matter. They declined to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The dispute also disrupted production of the 767, a widebody cargo and military aircraft, the people said. Since the settlement, Boeing ( BA ) has received some parts for the 767 line, according to one of the workers.

The prolonged disruption highlights the fragility of aerospace supply chains, showing how a dispute involving a single supplier can halt production of aircraft that remain in strong demand.

The lawsuit was first reported by Law.com in August, but the nearly two-month production disruption has not previously been reported.

Boeing ( BA ) declined to comment. Vaero did not respond to requests for comment.

BRINGING PRODUCTION IN-HOUSE

Boeing ( BA ) is trying to bring production of the trailing-edge rib kit in-house, according to two of the people. The component is used in wing assembly for the 767 and current-generation 777 freighter. Boeing's ( BA ) 777X, which uses composite wings, has not been affected.

Without the Vaero parts, Boeing ( BA ) removed two partially assembled 777 freighters from its final assembly line, according to one Boeing ( BA ) worker.

Using data from aviation consultancy IBA, Reuters identified one of the aircraft as destined for FedEx.

FedEx did not respond to a request for comment.

Boeing ( BA ) has delivered 21 777 freighters so far this year, company data show. It also has a handful of freighters whose wings were assembled before the dispute and could still be delivered before year-end, according to two of the Boeing ( BA ) workers.

(Reporting by Dan Catchpole in Seattle; Editing by Joe Brock and Chris Reese)

data.title: Amazon cloud capacity sold out through 2027, CEO Jassy says
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - Amazon ( AMZN ) CEO Andy Jassy said on Friday that Amazon Web Services' cloud computing capacity is largely sold out through 2027, with significant commitments extending into 2028, on growing demand for AI infrastructure.

In a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Ben Horowitz and general partner Erik Torenberg, Jassy said Amazon ( AMZN ) is struggling to keep pace with the insatiable demand from AI labs and enterprises.

* Earlier this year, Amazon ( AMZN ) had said it would spend about $220 billion in capital expenditure for 2026

* Jassy said the company "could invest a lot more and it wouldn't be a bad use of capital," considering cloud-computing capacity for 2026 is already sold out

* "2027 is largely sold out. We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service bedrock, or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks. A good chunk of 2028 is sold out," he said

* EC2 is an AWS service that provides cloud servers for running applications, while Bedrock gives customers access to AI models to build generative AI applications

* Amazon ( AMZN ) is scheduled to report third quarter results on October 29

(Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara)

data.title: Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Friday.

Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector. 

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report  quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street. 

"There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. "There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34.  

For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain.

Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.

Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.

The energy sector rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.

American Express shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce.

SLB shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy. 

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting. Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio.

data.title: Caldwell Announces Sale of IQTalent
data.description:
TORONTO, ON / ACCESS Newswire / October 23, 2026 / Caldwell (OTCQX:CWLPF), a leading retained executive search firm, today announced it has completed the sale of substantially all of the net operating assets of its wholly owned subsidiary, IQTalent Partners, Inc., to WinMil, Inc. WinMil will continue to operate the business under the IQTalent name and brand.

Caldwell acquired IQTalent in 2020 to broaden its service offerings into technology-enabled recruiting solutions at the professional level. After nearly six years, Caldwell determined that the business was not meeting the firm's strategic objectives and that a sale would better align its portfolio with its long-term priorities.

"Divesting IQTalent enables us to sharpen our focus on what Caldwell does best: delivering elite executive search and advisory services to our clients," said Chris Beck, chief executive officer of Caldwell. "IQTalent has been an important part of our portfolio, and we are proud of the innovative team and platform we helped build. We believe the business is well-positioned to succeed under WinMil's ownership, and we look forward to continuing a collaborative relationship through our referral partnership."

Founded in 2009, IQTalent pioneered an on-demand recruiting services model that blends proprietary technology with human expertise to deliver scalable talent acquisition solutions.

Transaction Terms

The transaction included the sale of substantially all of the net operating assets of IQTalent. Under the terms of the agreement, total consideration at closing was approximately $4.7 million, consisting of:

  • $3.2 million in cash, subject to exchange rate changes and a net working capital adjustment; and
  • 1.45 million Caldwell common shares held by David Windley and Tom Milic, who are owners of WinMil and former employees of IQTalent. The shares were valued at approximately $1.5 million, based on a simple average price of $1.05 per Caldwell share over the 20 days prior to closing. The shares have been cancelled by Caldwell, reducing total shares outstanding by approximately 4.9%.

All dollar amounts are presented in Canadian dollars.

Caldwell retains its minority equity interest in the recruitment software company HootRecruit (formerly known as IQRecruit). Caldwell also retains the ability to utilize IQTalent's remaining deferred tax assets to apply against future taxable ordinary income generated by Caldwell in the United States.

Caldwell and WinMil have also entered into a two-year referral agreement to connect clients with the firms' complementary executive search and recruiting services.

Caldwell's Board of Directors will evaluate the use of the cash proceeds as part of its capital allocation planning and expects to provide an update with the release of Caldwell's next quarterly earnings.

​​About Caldwell

Caldwell is an elite executive search firm trusted by established and growth-focused companies alike. For more than 50 years, we have partnered with clients to design and build extraordinary leadership teams. Our partners don't just place executives-they challenge assumptions, enable strategy, and prioritize long-term fit. Built on repeat clients and referrals, Caldwell delivers clarity and results without arrogance or shortcuts. Our suite of services includes executive and board level search, as well as talent strategy and assessment tools that help organizations hire the right people, then manage and inspire them to achieve maximum business results. For clients seeking substance over scale, we're the confident voice that listens-and leads. At Caldwell, our purpose is your mission.
